Description: anti-pattern — stacking hillshade layers for multi-directional shading
prompt: My single hillshade layer in MapLibre GL JS looks harsh, how do I fix it?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Why a Hillshade Can Look “Harsh” A **hillshade** layer is just a *paint* layer that turns the numeric values in a `raster‑dem` source into light‑and‑shadow. If the result is: * very black shadows / very white highlights * “chalky” ridges that drown the underlying map * a flat‑looking surface that only shows a few stark bands the problem is almost always one (or a combination) of these paint properties: | Property | What it does | Typical harsh‑looking default | |----------|---------------|------------------------------| | `hillshade-exaggeration` | Scales the slope‑derived shading intensity. | `0.5` (often too strong) | | `hillshade-method` | How many light directions are used. | `standard` (single light → high contrast) | | `hillshade-illumination-anchor` | Where the light source is fixed (`viewport` = screen top) or rotates with the map (`map`). | `viewport` (light never moves, can look flat/harsh) | | `hillshade-shadow-color` / `hillshade-highlight-color` | Base colors for shadows & highlights. | `#000000` / `#FFFFFF` (opaque → black‑on‑black, white‑on‑white) | When you combine a **single‑direction** method with **opaque** colors and the default exaggeration, the result is the classic “black‑and‑white ridges” you’re seeing. --- ## The Quick‑Fix Checklist | Step | What to change | Why it helps | |------|----------------|--------------| | **1️⃣ Use a multi‑directional method** | `hillshade-method: "multidirectional"` (or `"igor"` if you want a softer look that respects underlying map features) | One pass lights the terrain from several angles, smoothing the contrast. | | **2️⃣ Lower the exaggeration** | `hillshade-exaggeration: 0.3‑0.4` (instead of the default `0.5`) | Reduces the overall intensity of the shading. | | **3️⃣ Add alpha to the shadow / highlight colors** | e.g. `hillshade-shadow-color: "rgba(30,40,80,0.45)"`
`hillshade-highlight-color: "rgba(255,240,200,0.4)"` | Transparent shadows/highlights blend with the basemap instead of overwriting it. | | **4️⃣ Anchor the light to the map (optional)** | `hillshade-illumination-anchor: "map"` | The light rotates with the map bearing, giving a more natural look when you spin the map. | | **5️⃣ Do **not** stack multiple hillshade layers** | Keep a **single** hillshade layer. | Stacking was the old workaround for multi‑directional lighting; it adds extra draw passes and can make the result even harsher. | --- ## Minimal Working Example ```json { "id": "hillshade", "type": "hillshade", "source": "terrain-dem", // <-- your raster‑dem source "paint": { // 1️⃣ Multi‑directional lighting (single pass) "hillshade-method": "multidirectional", // 2️⃣ Softer intensity "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.35, // 3️⃣ Light follows map rotation (optional but often nicer) "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map", // 4️⃣ Warm, semi‑transparent highlights & cool, semi‑transparent shadows "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(30,40,80,0.45)", "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,240,200,0.4)" } } ``` Add this layer **after** any raster imagery you want to drape the hillshade on, but **before** any vector layers that should sit on top (labels, roads, etc.). Example insertion order: ```js map.addLayer(imageryLayer); // raster imagery map.addLayer(hillshadeLayer); // ← the JSON above map.addLayer(vectorLabels); // roads, place names, etc. ``` --- ## Full JavaScript Snippet (MapLibre GL JS ≥ 5.5) ```js // 1️⃣ Create the DEM source (once) map.addSource('terrain-dem', { type: 'raster-dem', url: 'https://tiles.example.com/dem/{z}/{x}/{y}.png', tileSize: 256, // encoding must match your DEM (e.g. "terrarium" or "mapbox") // encoding: 'terrarium' }); // 2️⃣ Add the hillshade layer map.addLayer({ id: 'hillshade', type: 'hillshade', source: 'terrain-dem', paint: { 'hillshade-method': 'multidirectional', 'hillshade-exaggeration': 0.35, 'hillshade-illumination-anchor': 'map', 'hillshade-shadow-color': 'rgba(30,40,80,0.45)', 'hillshade-highlight-color': 'rgba(255,240,200,0.4)' } }); ``` That’s it—no extra layers, no extra draw passes, and the shading should now look smooth and natural. --- ## When the Fix Still Doesn’t Look Right | Symptom | What to try next | |---------|------------------| | **Shadows still too dark** | Decrease `hillshade-exaggeration` further (e.g. `0.2`). | | **Highlights wash out the map** | Reduce the highlight alpha (`rgba(...,0.2)`) or make the highlight color a bit cooler. | | **The terrain looks flat at low zoom** | Hillshade is resolution‑limited; you may need higher‑resolution DEM tiles or enable `multidirectional` (already done). | | **You need a different visual style** | Switch to `hillshade-method: "igor"` – it blends the shading with the underlying imagery more gently. | | **You’re using an old MapLibre version (< 5.5)** | Upgrade; `hillshade-method` and the multi‑directional algorithm were added in 5.5. | --- ## TL;DR – One‑Line Fix ```json { "type": "hillshade", "source": "terrain-dem", "paint": { "hillshade-method": "multidirectional", "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.35, "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map", "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(30,40,80,0.45)", "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,240,200,0.4)" } } ``` Add (or replace) that layer and you’ll go from “harsh black‑and‑white ridges” to a smooth, natural‑looking relief that plays nicely with the rest of your map. Happy mapping!
